reports.title: Understanding Your Monthly Reports
reports.desc: For business owners: how to read the statements we send you every month — what each report says, the five checks worth doing, and how to get the most from your accounting team.

lessons.title: What arrives every month, and when
lessons.html:
By the 5th working day of each month, your statements for the previous month land in your portal — you'll see the announcement in your room, a 📬 card on your home page, and the pack itself under Documents. The pack contains your Profit & Loss (what you earned and spent), your Balance Sheet (what you own and owe), supporting schedules, and a short cover note — five lines from your accounting team telling you the month's story and anything they need from you.

Behind that delivery sits a monthly rhythm you mostly don't see: your transactions posted daily, every bank account reconciled to its statement, and a close checklist your team completes and signs before anything reaches you. When you tap ✓ Confirm receipt on the 📬 card, you're closing the loop — your team knows the pack reached you, and your records show when.

One habit, thirty seconds: when the pack arrives, read the cover note first. It's written to answer the question you were about to ask — and if it lists anything awaiting you (a question about a transaction, a document we need), handling it that day is what keeps next month's statements on time too.

TRY IT NOW: Open your Documents tab and find last month's pack. Read the cover note. If there's a 📬 card waiting on your home page, confirm receipt — that timestamp is yours as much as ours.

lessons.title: Reading your Profit & Loss
lessons.html:
The P&L answers one question: did the business make money this month? Read it top to bottom as a story:

  1. Revenue — everything you earned in the month (not everything that hit the bank — more on that in Lesson 3).
  2. Cost of sales — what the things you sold cost you. Revenue minus this is your gross profit, and the percentage (gross margin) is the single most watchable number in your business: if you sell at the same prices and margin falls, your costs rose or something is leaking.
  3. Operating expenses — rent, salaries, power, charges: the cost of existing for a month.
  4. The bottom line — profit or loss. One month's figure is weather; the trend across months is climate, and climate is what you steer by.

Your P&L always shows the previous month beside the current one. That comparison column is where the reading happens: big movements are either explained in the cover note already, or worth a question. "Why is cost of sales up 18%?" is exactly the kind of question your team hopes you'll ask — and has usually pre-answered.

What the P&L is not: it is not your bank balance. A profitable month can end with less cash (you paid old bills, bought stock, customers haven't paid you yet) and a loss-making month can end with more. The two reports answer different questions on purpose.

TRY IT NOW: On your latest P&L, find the line with the biggest change from last month. Is it explained in the cover note? If not — ask. That's what the room chat is for.

lessons.title: Reading your Balance Sheet
lessons.html:
If the P&L is the month's story, the Balance Sheet is a photograph of the business on the last day of it: what you own, what you owe, and what's left — and the quiet problems live here, which is why it rewards two minutes of attention.

What you own (assets): cash and bank balances (should feel familiar — if the bank figure surprises you, say so); receivables — money customers owe you (the schedule shows who and for how long; anything aging past your terms deserves a phone call from your side); stock; equipment.

What you owe (liabilities): suppliers awaiting payment; loans; and the tax accounts — VAT collected from your customers, PAYE deducted from staff, pension — which deserve a special sentence: that money was never yours. It sits in your bank looking like cash, but it belongs to FIRS, the state, and your staff's pension accounts. Your Balance Sheet keeps it visible precisely so it never gets spent by accident — one of the most valuable things monthly statements do for a small business.

What's left (equity): what the owners have in the business — capital put in plus profits kept. If you put personal money in or take money out, telling your team what it was (capital? a loan? drawings?) is what keeps this section true; it's why they sometimes ask about transfers from your personal account.

TRY IT NOW: Find receivables on your latest Balance Sheet and open the aging schedule beside it. Is anyone on that list a surprise? The oldest name is this week's phone call.

lessons.title: The five-minute monthly review
lessons.html:
You don't need an accounting course to read your pack well — you need five checks, five minutes, every month:

  1. Cover note first. The story, and anything awaiting you.
  2. Gross margin vs last month. Same prices but thinner margin = costs moved. Ask why if the note doesn't say.
  3. The biggest mover on the P&L. Find it; confirm you understand it.
  4. Receivables aging. Who owes you, how old — and who gets a call this week. (Steady sales with climbing receivables means you're selling well and collecting badly; caught early, it's a phone call, not a crisis.)
  5. The tax lines. VAT, PAYE, pension balances on the Balance Sheet — that's money already spoken for. If cash minus those figures looks thin, you've learned something important while it's still cheap to know.

Then, if anything raised an eyebrow: ask in the room. Questions make the service better, not slower — your team would far rather explain a number than have you quietly wonder about it. And the answer becomes part of your record, in the same place as everything else.

TRY IT NOW: Run the five checks on your latest pack — genuinely, now, it's five minutes. Post any question the checks raise in your room chat today.

lessons.title: Working with your accounting team
lessons.html:
A few things you'll see from us during the month, and how to get the best from each:

❓ Questions about transactions. When we meet a payment we can't place, an amber card appears on your portal home — and the same question arrives by email. Just reply to the email (or type in the card): your answer files itself, and the transaction gets posted correctly the same day. The faster these come back, the truer your books are all month — and unanswered ones do get a gentle automated reminder, so answering first time saves everyone the nudge.

📎 Documents we need. Bank statements and a few regulars, requested at the start of each month with a due date. Upload from the card, or reply to the email with the file attached — either way it lands in your Documents automatically. When these arrive early, your statements arrive early; when they're late, they are usually the whole reason statements are.

📬 The delivery ceremony. Statements ready → the card appears → you confirm receipt. Thirty seconds that gives both of us a permanent record of what was delivered and when.

Adding your people: your portal supports team members — your own bookkeeper or manager can be invited to the room, see the documents, and answer the transaction questions directly. Many of our smoothest engagements are ones where the owner reads the pack and their staff handle the cards. Ask us and we'll set it up.

And anything else — a decision coming up, a loan you're considering, a number you don't like — the room is the place. What's written there is remembered, actioned, and part of your engagement's permanent record.

TRY IT NOW: Check your portal home for any amber or green cards waiting. Clear them — then notice how little time it took versus how long they'd been sitting.
